t: Maximum Compatibility Score Sum -- Optimal Pairing With Bitmask DP
o: We must pair m students with m mentors one-to-one, maximizing the total number of identical answers per pair. Example 1 pairs student 0 with mentor 2, student 1 with mentor 0, and student 2 with mentor 1 for 3 + 2 + 3 = 8, beating every other perfect matching. Example 2 shows the floor: completely opposite answer sheets make every pair score 0. With m, n <= 8 there are at most 8! = 40320 matchings, so exhaustive search is feasible -- but recasting the assignment as a subset dynamic program removes redundant recomputation and scales far beyond these limits.
k: Precompute score[i][j], the number of equal answers between student i and mentor j; afterward the raw answer sheets are irrelevant.
Fixing the assignment order lets popcount(mask) identify the next student: once the mentors in mask are taken, exactly popcount(mask) students are placed.
dp[mask] stores the best total for pairing the first |mask| students with the mentor set mask, extended by removing one mentor per transition.

a.i: Recursively assign students in order, trying every unused mentor for the current student and undoing the choice afterwards. The m <= 8 bound keeps the factorial search tree tiny -- at most 8! = 40320 leaves -- so this straightforward search passes easily.
s: Precompute the compatibility score of every student-mentor pair.
Recursively place student i with each unused mentor, tracking usage in a boolean array (or bitmask).
Add the pair score, recurse to student i + 1, and take the maximum over all choices.
Return 0 once every student is placed; the top-level call yields the answer.
a.t: O(m^2 * n + m! * m) -- precomputing all pair scores plus a factorial-size search with m branches per level
a.sp: O(m^2 + m) -- the score matrix and the recursion stack

a.n: Approach 2: Bitmask Dynamic Programming Over Mentors
a.i: Let dp[mask] be the best score pairing the first popcount(mask) students with exactly the mentors in mask. Processing masks in increasing order guarantees every submask is ready; trying each mentor j inside mask extends dp[mask without j] by score[nextStudent][j]. This shares overlapping states that plain backtracking recomputes.
s: Build the score matrix as before.
Initialize dp[0] = 0 and iterate masks from 1 to 2^m - 1.
Let i = popcount(mask) - 1 be the student newly paired at this state.
For each mentor j in mask, set dp[mask] = max(dp[mask], dp[mask ^ (1 << j)] + score[i][j]).
a.t: O(m^2 * n + 2^m * m) -- score precomputation plus one transition per (state, mentor) pair
a.sp: O(2^m) -- a table over all mentor subsets

w: With m <= 8 both approaches run instantly: present backtracking first for clarity, then offer bitmask DP as the pattern that survives much larger m (up to roughly 20) and adapts to variants like minimizing mismatch cost. Pitfalls: tying student i to popcount(mask) - 1 is what makes the DP sound -- letting students jump around breaks correctness; parenthesize shift-and-mask checks in C++ to dodge precedence surprises. Edge case: m = 1 simply returns the single pair score. Classic follow-up: reconstruct the optimal assignment by storing argmax predecessors.
